points.en: Biographical preaching is preaching a Bible truth through the life of a Bible person, so that the life displays the truth rather than the man being the subject.
Scripture itself does this: Hebrews 11 holds up one life after another, or 1 Corinthians 10:11 says these lives were written down as examples and warnings for us.
People are interested in people, so a truth embodied in a life becomes concrete, personal and memorable for the hearer.
Biography gives the hearer both examples to follow and warnings to heed.
A single life shows God's dealings and faithfulness over time, or lets the hearer watch a person change by grace.
As an illustration: a brief reference to the character dropped under a point in another sermon, suited to a life that merely confirms a point already being made.
As explanation and illustration: a fuller treatment forming a whole movement of the sermon, suited to a life rich enough to carry a major part of the message.
As a complete sermon: the entire message built on one life studied in depth, suited to a life that embodies the whole truth being preached.
The whole sermon is built on one story and its cast (Ahab, Jezebel, Naboth, Elijah in 1 Kings 21), retold from beginning to end under one theme: sin will be paid its wages, Payday, Someday.
Its power is that vivid narrative and the thundering truth are one, so the hearers experience the scene rather than hearing a bare point, and it keeps its force when preached again and again.
The sermon lets the injustice stand unanswered until Elijah's verdict, so the shape of the story dictates the shape of the sermon.
The chief danger is moralizing: reducing a life to a lesson in behavior (be like Daniel, do not be like Lot) so the gospel becomes self-improvement.
The cure is to let every life, even a warning, point beyond itself to God and to Christ and his grace, driving the hearer to the Savior.
Study the person's history and why he matters, his relationships, and what became of him in the end and why.
Search out where else Scripture mentions him, and listen to his words and silences, weighing the places and events that shaped him.
The aim is a clear, text-based portrait of the person that the preacher can make others see.
The sermon names a Bible character and states the central truth of God that his life displays, as the point of the sermon.
It sketches the life's arc (or a theme running through it) to be retold faithfully and vividly, rather than forced into an artificial grid.
It shows how the sermon points beyond the person to God, Christ and grace, so it does not merely say imitate or avoid this person.
People are drawn to people, and a truth embodied in a life is concrete, memorable and felt, where an abstract statement slides away.
This fits how God revealed himself: not only as propositions or attributes but in a Person, the Word made flesh, so truth is seen lived.
Agree that moralizing is a real danger, but reply that true biographical preaching is different: it carries a Bible truth rather than a moral tacked on.
True biographical preaching studies the life carefully and retells it faithfully and vividly.
Its truth finally points to Christ and grace, so the gospel is revealed through the life (as in Hebrews 11 or Payday Someday).
The sustained study of a person in the Bible Characters courses (history, relationships, words, end) is the raw material for a biographical sermon; the same discipline is used.
The student turns the study into a sermon by choosing a treatment (illustration, explanation, or complete sermon) and retelling the life vividly.
The sermon must land a truth that points to Christ, so that study becomes proclamation.
